title: the breath again — every claim checked
hook: breath gets asked to carry cures, hacks and hidden energies; this stretch checks every claim against the page
carry: the breath again — every claim checked
tomorrow: the breath again — every claim checked

segments.voice: Last week closed on sleep: the temple's bedtime and its dawn song, Rama woken with words. Did you end the day gently, or wake someone with words instead of a jolt? Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

A sticky note on a bathroom mirror says: just breathe. Fair enough. But breath gets asked to carry a lot more than that these days. One trick to fix your sleep. One pattern to melt stress away. An ancient secret energy, now in an app. Some of it may help. Some of it is said with more confidence than the evidence has earned. These last days of the Ayurveda lens come back to the breath, and they come with a promise written into the title. Today: the breath again, every claim checked.
screen: `JUST BREATHE.` → `A TRICK, A PATTERN, A SECRET.` → `EVERY CLAIM CHECKED.`

segments.voice: Start with the rule for these days. Every claim about breath gets one of three labels. The text says: a line you can find on the page, with a reference. Tradition says: what teachers and families pass down, honored, but not the same as the page. And a doctor decides: anything about illness, cure or treatment. This path won't promise a cure. Now one claim, checked. The Yoga Sutras of Patanjali, in the second chapter, describe the breath in practice. In paraphrase: its movement out, its movement in, and its pause, when watched by place, by time and by number, becomes long and fine. The Sanskrit for that last pair is dirgha sukshma, long and subtle. Look at what kind of claim that is. It isn't a promise about blood pressure or sleep. It's a description of what happens to breath under attention, and it hands over the method: notice where the breath is felt, how long it lasts, how many there are. That's a claim anyone can check, gently, by watching. Label: the text says, and the watching is yours. Now look at what the sutra doesn't say. It doesn't say breathe in a special pattern to heal. It doesn't offer a number of seconds. Those come from other texts and other teachers, and when they come up on these days they'll get their own labels. One plain safety line, because breath work isn't neutral. Anyone with a heart or lung condition, anyone pregnant, anyone who gets dizzy or anxious with breath exercises, keeps to easy natural breathing and asks a doctor before any holding of the breath. Today's practice holds nothing. It only watches.
screen: `THREE LABELS FOR EVERY CLAIM` · `WATCHED BY PLACE, TIME AND NUMBER` · `DIRGHA SUKSHMA: LONG AND FINE` · `WHAT THE SUTRA DOESN'T SAY`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: watch, don't steer. Sit comfortably and let the breath do whatever it's doing. First, place: where is it felt most? The nostrils, the chest, the belly. Just find the spot. Then time: does the breath in take longer than the breath out, or the same? No changing it. Then number: count a few breaths, one to five, and start again. If it grows longer and finer on its own, notice that. If it doesn't, notice that too. Both are honest results. If you pray, you can let the breath be your prayer. The bell holds the time.
The breath again. In the Yoga Sutras, breath watched by place, time and number becomes long and fine: a claim you can check by watching. Today's word.

Your line: the breath again — every claim checked. Today, catch yourself breathing once without changing it, and when you hear a claim about breath, give it a label. Day one thousand three hundred twenty-one.

howItsDone: Some yoga teachers who follow Patanjali have students watch the breath before regulating it, and adapt or skip breath-holding for students with health conditions.

fork.setup: a friend says an old text proves a breathing trick cures anxiety. what do you ask first?
options: which text, and what does the page actually say?
nothing: old texts are always right.
fork.reveal: find the page first. the Yoga Sutra on breath describes it growing long and fine under attention, and promises no cure. anything about illness, a doctor decides.

original.note: Sanskrit dirgha sukshma: long and subtle. Yoga Sutra 2.50's description of breath watched by place, time and number.

trapdoor: what you thought: ancient texts promise that the right breathing cures everything.
what it means: the Yoga Sutra describes breath, watched by place, time and number, becoming long and fine. a description, not a cure.
what a scholar hears: desha, kala, sankhya and dirgha sukshma in sutra 2.50, with no count of seconds; the patterns come from other texts.
recall: a warrior, and a daughter coming home
